title: SpaceX Just Launched 29 Satellites—and the Booster Has Flown 18 Times!
summary: Have you ever watched a rocket launch and land itself? SpaceX did it again! On August 11, a Falcon 9 rocket blasted off from Florida carrying 29 Starlink satellites. These satellites are part of a huge network that beams internet down to Earth. About eight and a half minutes after liftoff, the rocket's first stage came back down and landed perfectly on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. The ship has a funny name: "A Shortfall of Gravitas." But here's the really cool part: this was the 18th flight for that same booster! Imagine reusing a rocket almost 20 times. This booster, called B1085, has done many Starlink missions, but it also launched astronauts to the International Space Station in 2024 and sent a crew on a polar orbit mission called Fram2. The upper part of the rocket kept going and released the satellites about an hour after launch. This was SpaceX's 93rd Falcon 9 launch this year, and 72 of those were for Starlink. There are now more than 10,900 active Starlink satellites circling Earth. SpaceX wants to eventually have 100,000 bigger satellites, and Elon Musk even dreams of launching a million! That's a lot of hardware in space, but for now, each launch brings faster internet to more places on our planet.
why_it_matters: Reusable rockets like this make space travel cheaper, which could someday help astronauts go to the Moon or Mars, and also bring fast internet to kids in remote areas around the world.

background_read: Most rockets used to be thrown away after one flight, but SpaceX proved it can reuse the first stage over and over to save money and time between launches.
Starlink satellites form a mega-constellation that beams high-speed internet to remote places like mountains, deserts, and even planes at sea, where regular cables can't reach.
A booster named B1085 also flew the Fram2 mission earlier, which was a special polar orbit trip—something rarely done with human crews because it requires more fuel and planning.
Article_Structure: WHO: SpaceX, the rocket company, and its Falcon 9 booster named B1085.
WHAT: The 18th launch and landing of the same booster, carrying 29 Starlink internet satellites into orbit.
WHERE: Launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and landed on the drone ship 'A Shortfall of Gravitas' in the Atlantic Ocean.
WHY: To grow the Starlink network for global internet and to keep proving reusable rockets make space travel cheaper and more frequent.

perspectives.description: Feels proud that reusing a rocket 18 times proves their technology works reliably and saves millions of dollars, pushing spaceflight forward.
Worries that a huge number of satellites could clutter space, make the night sky brighter, and increase the risk of dangerous collisions in orbit.

perspectives.perspective: A student in a rural area
perspectives.description: Excited because Starlink could finally bring fast, reliable internet to his village where laying cables is impossible, helping with homework and connecting to the world.
Feels pressure to develop reusability fast as well, since landing boosters and flying them again changes the space industry and makes it harder to keep up.
